stem:
Three bar magnets were arranged as shown. Each magnet is attracted to the magnet it touches. Pole A is a north pole.

Which poles are south poles?
working: A = N so B = S. B attracts C, so C = N and D = S. D attracts E, so E = N and F = S. South poles: B, D, F.
Watch out: Flip at every touching join. Write the letter on every end before choosing.

distractors.2: C touches the south pole B, so C must be north.
distractors.3: C and E are north poles.
distractors.4: E touches the south pole D, so E is north.

stem:
Magnets P and Q are placed on a table. Magnet Q is held in place.

What happens to magnet P when it is let go?
options: P does not move, because magnets only attract iron.
working: P's south pole faces Q's south pole. Like poles repel, so P is pushed away from Q.
Watch out: Look only at the two ends that FACE each other.

distractors.1: That would need unlike poles facing (N facing S).
distractors.2: Magnets also attract and repel other magnets.
distractors.3: Q is held in place, so it cannot move.

stem: Siti tried to make magnets in four different ways. Which one will become the strongest magnet?
working: Steel is magnetic. One-direction strokes make a magnet, and 50 strokes make a stronger magnet than 30.
Watch out: The biggest number is a trap twice here: (2) uses the wrong method and (4) the wrong material.

distractors.1: Correct method, but fewer strokes than (3).
distractors.2: Back-and-forth strokes undo each other — even 80 strokes make a very weak magnet.
distractors.4: Copper is not a magnetic material, so it can never become a magnet.

stem:
Marcus wrote some statements about making a magnet by the stroke method.

A The magnet must be stroked in one direction only.
B The more strokes, the stronger the magnet made.
C An aluminium rod can be made into a magnet if it is stroked enough times.
D The magnet is lifted away from the nail at the end of each stroke.
working: A, B and D describe the stroke method. C is false: aluminium is not a magnetic material.
Watch out: Mark each statement T or F first, then find the matching option.

distractors.1: Leaves out D — lifting the magnet away is part of the method.
distractors.3: Includes the false statement C and leaves out A.

stem:
Three rings, X, Y and Z, were placed on a wooden rod as shown.

Which statement is **definitely** true?
options: Z is made of a non-magnetic material.
X and Z repel each other.
working: Y floats above X, so they push each other away — only two magnets can repel. Z just sits on Y: it could be a magnet, a magnetic material or even non-magnetic resting there, so (1) and (2) cannot be sure.
Watch out: 'Definitely' means it MUST be true. A gap proves two magnets; touching proves nothing.

distractors.1: Z touches Y — touching tells us nothing for sure.
distractors.2: Z might be attracted to Y, so it might be magnetic. Not possible to tell.
distractors.3: X and Z are not facing each other.

notes: Figure rendered from figure_spec on 27 Oct by scripts/render-figures.ts; founder to check it.

stem:
A compass was placed next to the north pole of a bar magnet. The dark end of the compass needle is its north-seeking pole.

Which diagram shows the compass needle correctly?
working: The compass needle is a small magnet. Its north (dark) end is repelled by the magnet's north pole, so the dark end points away; its south end turns towards the magnet.
Watch out: A compass needle is a magnet — use like-repel, unlike-attract on its two ends.

distractors.1: That is where it points with no magnet nearby.
distractors.2: The dark (north) end would be repelled, not attracted, by a north pole.
distractors.4: The needle lines up with the magnet, not at a slant.

stem:
Three ring magnets, A, B and C, were placed on a wooden rod as shown. The top face of A is a north pole.

(a) Name the poles at face P and face Q.

Face P:
Face Q:
working: Reasoning: B floats above A, so the faces facing each other are like poles: P is north like A's top face. The other face of the same magnet is the opposite pole, so Q is south.
Common error: Writing P = south because 'opposites attract' — but a gap means they REPEL.

stem:
Three ring magnets, A, B and C, were placed on a wooden rod as shown. The top face of A is a north pole.

(b) Marcus pushed ring C down gently and let go. Predict what happens to C. Explain.
answer: C moves back up (and floats again). The bottom of C and face Q are **like poles**, which **repel**.
working: Claim: C springs back up.
Evidence: C was floating above B before it was pushed.
Reasoning: Like poles of B and C face each other and repel.

stem:
Siti stroked four similar steel needles, A to D, in one direction only. She counted the pins each needle attracted.

| Needle | Number of strokes | Number of pins attracted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 10 | 2 |
| B | 20 | 5 |
| C | 30 | 7 |
| D | 40 | 9 |

(a) State the relationship between the number of strokes and the number of pins attracted.
answer: As the number of strokes **increases**, the number of pins attracted **increases**.
working: Common error: Only naming the best needle ('D attracted the most').

stem:
Siti stroked four similar steel needles, A to D, in one direction only. She counted the pins each needle attracted.

| Needle | Number of strokes | Number of pins attracted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 10 | 2 |
| B | 20 | 5 |
| C | 30 | 7 |
| D | 40 | 9 |

(b) Siti stroked another steel needle, E, 40 times, moving the magnet backwards and forwards. E attracted only 1 pin. Explain why E attracted fewer pins than D.
answer: E was stroked **back and forth (in both directions)** while D was stroked **in one direction only**. Strokes in opposite directions undo each other, so E became a much weaker magnet even with the same number of strokes.
working: Claim: E is a weaker magnet because the method was wrong.
Evidence: Same number of strokes (40) as D, but back-and-forth instead of one direction.
Reasoning: The stroke method only works when stroking in one direction; back-and-forth strokes cancel out.

stem:
A crane at a scrapyard uses an electromagnet to lift steel scraps and drop them into a lorry.

(a) Why is an electromagnet more useful than a bar magnet for this job?
answer: It can be **switched off**, so the crane can **drop** the steel scraps where it wants.

stem:

(b) Suggest one way to make the electromagnet lift more steel scraps at one time.
answer: Increase the **number of turns** of wire, or use **more batteries**.
